newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan hostages say situation becoming dangerous.
newsitem.headline: Japan hostages say situation becoming dangerous.

text.p: Japanese held captive in the Lima hostage siege pleaded on Sunday with their prime minister to find a quick end to the stand-off because their situation was becoming more dangerous.

In a letter to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto carried out by nine Japanese hostages released earlier on Sunday, the still captive Japanese, numbering about 20 diplomats and businessmen, said they wanted to be freed as quickly as possible.

"If this bad precedent is left as it is, it could have a serious effect on the future economic activities of both Peru and Japan, and we are anxious to see it resolved as early as possible," the letter said.

In a separate letter, captive Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, whose residence was taken over by Marxist rebels on December 17, also urged Japanese authorities to solve the crisis at an "early date", foreign ministry officials said.

The Japanese are the biggest group of non-Peruvians held by about 20 members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement who took over the residence during a party to celebrate Japanese Emperor Akihito's 63rd birthday. The rebels still hold 83 of nearly 500 guests first captured in last week's assault.
The two letters were carried out by nine Japanese among 20 hostages who the rebels freed on Saturday.

While acknowledging their captors were treating them properly, the letter to the prime minister said: "But if the situation in which heavily-armed soldiers keep a close watch on us lasts for a long time, it will become extremely difficult for us to keep the balance between mind and body."

"This situation is getting more dangerous day by day," the letter added. "We ask you (Prime Minister Hashimoto) to make a stronger request to the Peruvian government urgently to set free all the Japanese held as hostages at an early date."
Hashimoto told reporters the message, which he said was probably written under scrutiny of the rebels, pained him and indicated the "tough situation" faced by the hostages.
Hashimoto said he planned to contact Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, who is of Japanese ancestry, to see if there was any way negotiations could be speeded up.

"It is not time yet to get our hopes up but reading the guerrillas' demands, it seems possible to have a dialogue with the rebels," Hashimoto said. "We will not yield to terror, and will not change in our efforts toward a peaceful solution."

In other developments on the Japan end of the siege, the Foreign Ministry advised Japanese not to travel to Lima and a senior official said there would be no change in Tokyo's aid plans for Peru because of the crisis.
A ministry statement said in the present circumstances the safety of visitors to Lima could not be guaranteed.
On the aid front, a senior foreign ministry official told reporters Japan would maintain at present levels its assistance to Peru which is the biggest recipient in Latin America.
"We will continue what we are doing right now. We are not considering any alteration to our policy," the official said.
He rejected criticism by the rebels that Japanese aid to Peru was flawed because it did not help the people most in need and was solely for the benefit of Japanese companies.

"Speculation is rife that Japan's Peru aid policy was wrong, but I don't think that is the case," the official said. "What we are doing is intended to root out poverty, and I'm pretty sure Peruvian people understand this well."
